learning_objective: 🎯 Understand the anatomy, tuning principles, and cultural significance of major melodic instruments like the Tanpura (the drone) and the Sitar.

key_vocabulary.definition: A four-stringed drone instrument that provides the base pitch (Sa) for singers and instrumentalists.
The large, hollow, pumpkin-shaped resonator at the base of string instruments.
The bridge of the instrument, crafted precisely to produce a rich, buzzing, overtone-heavy sound.
A wire plectrum worn on the index finger to pluck the strings of a Sitar.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: The Tanpura does not play melody; it provides a continuous harmonic drone. Key parts include: Tumba (resonator gourd), Dand (long wooden neck), Tabli (wooden cover over the Tumba), Jawari (bridge), Khunti (tuning pegs), and Manka (small beads for fine-tuning).

The Tanpura has 4 strings. The 1st string is tuned to Mandra Pa (low Pa) for most ragas, or Mandra Ma (low Ma) if Pa is forbidden (like in Malkauns). The 2nd and 3rd strings (Jodi strings) are tuned to Madhya Sa (middle Sa). The 4th string is tuned to Mandra Sa (low Sa).

A fretted plucked string instrument. Unlike the Tanpura, the Sitar has curved, movable frets (Pardas) tied to the Dand. It has main playing strings, drone strings (Chikari) used for rhythm, and sympathetic resonance strings (Tarab) underneath the frets that vibrate automatically to add richness.

fun_activity.title: 🧵 The Thread of Buzz (Jiva)
fun_activity.instructions: Did you know that Tanpura players slip a tiny cotton thread between the strings and the bridge (Jawari)? This tiny thread creates the rich, buzzing overtone (the 'Jiva' or life of the sound). Without this thread, the Tanpura would sound like a flat guitar string!

exam_tips: 📌 Learn to draw a simple, labeled diagram of the Tanpura (Tumba, Tabli, Bridge, Dand, Khunti). It fetches guaranteed marks.
📌 Always mention the tuning of the 4 strings of the Tanpura clearly: Pa (or Ma/Ni), Sa, Sa, low Sa.
📌 Highlight that the Tanpura is a drone instrument (no frets), while the Sitar is a melody instrument (has frets).
quick_recap: ⭐ The 'Manka' (fine-tuning bead) is moved up to decrease the pitch and down to increase the pitch.
⭐ Sitar frets are curved so that the player can pull the string sideways to execute 'Meend' (glides) over multiple notes.
⭐ The mesmerizing buzz of Indian string instruments is scientifically caused by the flat, slightly curved design of the 'Jawari' (bridge).
